claim: DolP (formerly YraP) is a protein of unresolved structure and function.
source: Some virulence factors serve to maintain the integrity of the outer membrane, including DolP (formerly YraP) a protein of unresolved structure and function.
evidence: The abstract directly states that DolP's structure and function were unresolved prior to this study.

claim: Loss of DolP increases membrane fluidity.
source: Here, we reveal DolP is a lipoprotein functionally conserved amongst Gram-negative bacteria and that loss of DolP increases membrane fluidity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: DolP is composed of two BON domains that form an interconnected opposing pair.
source: We present the NMR solution structure for Escherichia coli DolP, which is composed of two BON domains that form an interconnected opposing pair.
evidence: The abstract states this structural finding, which is supported by NMR data and structural analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: The C-terminal BON domain of DolP binds anionic phospholipids through an extensive membrane:protein interface.
source: The C-terminal BON domain binds anionic phospholipids through an extensive membrane:protein interface.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data and structural modeling shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Phospholipid binding is essential for DolP function.
source: This interaction is essential for DolP function and is required for sub-cellular localisation of the protein to the cell division site, providing evidence of subcellular localisation of these phospholipids within the outer membrane.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by mutagenesis and complementation assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Phospholipid binding is required for sub-cellular localisation of DolP to the cell division site.
source: This interaction is essential for DolP function and is required for sub-cellular localisation of the protein to the cell division site, providing evidence of subcellular localisation of these phospholipids within the outer membrane.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Gram-negative outer-membrane functions as a permeability barrier against antibiotics, detergents, and environmental stresses.
source: The Gram-negative outer-membrane envelops the bacterium and functions as a permeability barrier against antibiotics, detergents, and environmental stresses.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established scientific knowledge about bacterial outer membranes.

claim: Loss of DolP results in the disruption of OM integrity.
source: Loss of DolP results in the disruption of OM integrity, induces increased susceptibility to detergents and antibiotics, and attenuates the virulence of Salmonella enterica (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and by experimental data in Figure 1C showing sensitivity to vancomycin and SDS.

claim: Loss of DolP induces increased susceptibility to detergents and antibiotics.
source: Loss of DolP results in the disruption of OM integrity, induces increased susceptibility to detergents and antibiotics, and attenuates the virulence of Salmonella enterica (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Loss of DolP attenuates the virulence of Salmonella enterica.
source: Loss of DolP results in the disruption of OM integrity, induces increased susceptibility to detergents and antibiotics, and attenuates the virulence of Salmonella enterica (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Morris et al., 2018.

claim: DolP is a crucial component of the serogroup B meningococcal vaccine where it enhances the immunogenicity of other components.
source: Importantly, DolP is a crucial component of the serogroup B meningococcal vaccine where it enhances the immunogenicity of other components by an unknown mechanism (Bos et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bos et al., 2014.

claim: The dolP gene was connected genetically to the activation of peptidoglycan amidases during E. coli cell division.
source: Recently, the dolP gene was connected genetically to the activation of peptidoglycan amidases during E. coli cell division, however this activity has not been directly confirmed experimentally (Tsang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsang et al., 2017, but the text notes this has not been directly confirmed experimentally.

claim: Protein interactome studies suggest DolP is a component of the β-barrel assembly machine (Bam) complex.
source: In contrast, protein interactome studies suggest DolP is a component of the β-barrel assembly machine (Bam) complex (Carlson et al., 2019; Babu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carlson et al., 2019 and Babu et al., 2018.

claim: In E. coli, the dolP gene is located downstream of the genes encoding LpoA, YraN, and DiaA.
source: In E. coli, the dolP gene is located downstream of the genes encoding LpoA (an activator of PBP1A) (Typas et al., 2010), YraN (a putative Holiday-Junction resolvase), and DiaA (a regulator of chromosomal replication) (Ishida et al., 2004), and two σE-dependent promoters are found immediately upstream of the dolP gene (Dartigalongue et al., 2001; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and by the genomic context diagram shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two σE-dependent promoters are found immediately upstream of the dolP gene.
source: In E. coli, the dolP gene is located downstream of the genes encoding LpoA (an activator of PBP1A) (Typas et al., 2010), YraN (a putative Holiday-Junction resolvase), and DiaA (a regulator of chromosomal replication) (Ishida et al., 2004), and two σE-dependent promoters are found immediately upstream of the dolP gene (Dartigalongue et al., 2001; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dartigalongue et al., 2001 and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DolP is predicted to encode a lipoprotein with two putative BON domains.
source: Bioinformatic analyses predicted that dolP encodes a lipoprotein with two putative domains of unknown function, termed BON domains (Yeats and Bateman, 2003), as well as a Lol-dependent OM targeting signal sequence where acylation was predicted to occur on cysteine residue C19.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis and a citation to Yeats and Bateman, 2003.

claim: DolP has a Lol-dependent OM targeting signal sequence where acylation was predicted to occur on cysteine residue C19.
source: Bioinformatic analyses predicted that dolP encodes a lipoprotein with two putative domains of unknown function, termed BON domains (Yeats and Bateman, 2003), as well as a Lol-dependent OM targeting signal sequence where acylation was predicted to occur on cysteine residue C19.
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic prediction and is experimentally validated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DolP was found in the Triton X-100 insoluble fraction of the E. coli cell envelope along with other OM proteins.
source: DolP was found in the Triton X-100 insoluble fraction of the E. coli cell envelope along with other OM proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of a C19A point mutant effectively eliminated DolP from the OM fractions.
source: Furthermore, expression of a C19A point mutant, preventing N-terminal acylation, effectively eliminated DolP from the OM fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DolP was not accessible to antibody or protease in intact E. coli cells.
source: Unlike the lipoproteins BamC and Lpp, which can be surface localized (Cowles et al., 2011; Webb et al., 2012), DolP was not accessible to antibody or protease in intact E. coli cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D and by citations.

claim: DolP could be labelled and degraded when OM integrity was compromised.
source: However, DolP could be labelled and degraded when OM integrity was compromised (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), confirming that DolP is predominantly targeted to the inner leaflet of the OM, localizing it within the periplasmic space.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: DolP is predominantly targeted to the inner leaflet of the OM, localizing it within the periplasmic space.
source: However, DolP could be labelled and degraded when OM integrity was compromised (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), confirming that DolP is predominantly targeted to the inner leaflet of the OM, localizing it within the periplasmic space.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing DolP is only accessible when the OM is permeabilized.

claim: The DolP lipoprotein is conserved across diverse species of Proteobacteria.
source: Further in silico analyses revealed the DolP lipoprotein was conserved across diverse species of Proteobacteria and is present even in organisms with highly-reduced genomes for example Buchnera spp (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Table 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: DolP is present even in organisms with highly-reduced genomes such as Buchnera spp.
source: Further in silico analyses revealed the DolP lipoprotein was conserved across diverse species of Proteobacteria and is present even in organisms with highly-reduced genomes for example Buchnera spp (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Table 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The genome of E. coli contains three BON-domain-containing proteins: DolP, OsmY, and Kbp.
source: The genome of E. coli contains three BON-domain-containing proteins: DolP, OsmY, and Kbp.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DolP shares a dual BON-domain architecture and 29.5% sequence identity with OsmY.
source: DolP shares a dual BON-domain architecture and 29.5% sequence identity with OsmY, which is distinguished from DolP by a canonical Sec-dependent signal sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: OsmY is distinguished from DolP by a canonical Sec-dependent signal sequence.
source: DolP shares a dual BON-domain architecture and 29.5% sequence identity with OsmY, which is distinguished from DolP by a canonical Sec-dependent signal sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Kbp consists of single BON and LysM domains and lacks a discernible signal sequence.
source: In contrast, Kbp consists of single BON and LysM domains and lacks a discernible signal sequence (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Clustering analyses revealed DolP, OsmY and Kbp are distributed throughout the α, β, and γ-proteobacteria and form distinct clusters.
source: Clustering analyses of sequences obtained by HMMER searches revealed DolP, OsmY and Kbp are distributed throughout the α, β, and γ-proteobacteria and form distinct clusters indicating that DolP has a role that is independent of OsmY and Kbp (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DolP has a role that is independent of OsmY and Kbp.
source: Clustering analyses of sequences obtained by HMMER searches revealed DolP, OsmY and Kbp are distributed throughout the α, β, and γ-proteobacteria and form distinct clusters indicating that DolP has a role that is independent of OsmY and Kbp (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from clustering analysis and supported by functional data showing OsmY and Kbp do not complement dolP mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: OsmY and Kbp are not functionally redundant with DolP.
source: Our analyses demonstrated that OsmY and Kbp are not functionally redundant with DolP and isogenic mutants show distinct phenotypes, therefore confirming a distinct role for DolP in E. coli (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: E. coli ΔdolP is susceptible to vancomycin, SDS, cholate, and deoxycholate.
source: Further evidence of a role for DolP in maintaining OM integrity is shown by E. coli ΔdolP susceptibility to vancomycin, SDS, cholate, and deoxycholate (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Resistance to vancomycin and SDS could be restored by supplying dolP in trans.
source: Resistance could be restored by supplying dolP in trans (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The growth rate observed for the dolP mutant strain was identical to that of the parent.
source: Despite evidence for disrupted OM integrity, the growth rate observed for the dolP mutant strain was identical to that of the parent, and scanning-electron microscopy revealed no obvious differences in cell size or shape (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C.

claim: Scanning-electron microscopy revealed no obvious differences in cell size or shape between parent and dolP mutant.
source: Despite evidence for disrupted OM integrity, the growth rate observed for the dolP mutant strain was identical to that of the parent, and scanning-electron microscopy revealed no obvious differences in cell size or shape (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,C.

claim: DolP homologues from S. enterica, V. cholerae, P. multocida, H. influenza, and N. meningitidis restore the OM barrier function of the E. coli ΔdolP mutant.
source: To determine whether DolP is broadly required for OM homeostasis, plasmids expressing DolP homologues from S. enterica, Vibrio cholerae, Pasteurella multocida, Haemophilus influenza, and Neisseria meningitidis were shown to restore the OM barrier function of the E. coli ΔdolP mutant (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D (labeled as 1F in text).

claim: Replacement of the DolP signal sequence with that of PelB prevented complementation of the ΔdolP phenotype.
source: Finally, either replacement of the DolP signal sequence with that of PelB (Tsang et al., 2017), which targets the protein to the periplasmic space, or mutation of the signal sequence to avoid OM targeting via the Lol system, prevented complementation of the ΔdolP phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and a citation.

claim: Mutation of the signal sequence to avoid OM targeting via the Lol system prevented complementation of the ΔdolP phenotype.
source: Finally, either replacement of the DolP signal sequence with that of PelB (Tsang et al., 2017), which targets the protein to the periplasmic space, or mutation of the signal sequence to avoid OM targeting via the Lol system, prevented complementation of the ΔdolP phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Localisation of DolP to the inner leaflet of the OM is essential to mediate its function.
source: Together these results support a conserved role for DolP in maintenance of OM integrity throughout Gram-negative bacteria and demonstrate that localisation of DolP to the inner leaflet of the OM is essential to mediate this function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that mistargeting DolP prevents complementation.

claim: Purified DolP was processed, soluble and monomeric.
source: Purified DolP was processed, soluble and monomeric, as confirmed by analytical ultra-centrifugation and size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The individual BON1 and BON2 domains have C-alpha backbone root mean square deviations (RMSDs) of 0.3 and 0.3 Å, respectively.
source: The individual BON1 (Residues 45–112) and BON2 (Residues 114–193) domains have C-alpha backbone root mean square deviations (RMSDs) of 0.3 and 0.3 Å, respectively, and an overall global RMSD of 0.5 Å (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural statistics shown in Table 2.

claim: DolP has an overall global RMSD of 0.5 Å.
source: The individual BON1 (Residues 45–112) and BON2 (Residues 114–193) domains have C-alpha backbone root mean square deviations (RMSDs) of 0.3 and 0.3 Å, respectively, and an overall global RMSD of 0.5 Å (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural statistics shown in Table 2.

claim: Each BON domain consists of a three-stranded mixed parallel/antiparallel β-sheet packed against two α-helices yielding an αββαβ topology.
source: Despite having low sequence identity (24.7%) each BON domain consists of a three-stranded mixed parallel/antiparallel β-sheet packed against two α-helices yielding an αββαβ topology.
evidence: This claim is supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The two BON domains present high structural homology and superpose with an RMSD of 1.8 Å over C-alpha backbone.
source: The two BON domains present high structural homology and superpose with an RMSD of 1.8 Å over C-alpha backbone (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: BON1 is embellished by an additional short α1* helix between BON1:α1 and BON1:β1.
source: Notably, BON1 is embellished by an additional short α1* helix between BON1:α1 and BON1:β1 (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The N-terminal acylation site is connected through a 27 amino acid dynamic unstructured linker.
source: The N-terminal acylation site is connected through a 27 amino acid dynamic unstructured linker (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data and S2 order parameter analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The experimentally determined scattering curve fit the NMR-derived structure with a χ of 1.263.
source: The experimentally determined scattering curve fit the NMR-derived structure with a χ (Konovalova et al., 2017) of 1.263, confirming the accuracy of the NMR-derived structure and an exclusively monomeric state (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The two BON domains pack against each other via their β-sheets through contacts mediated directly by Y75 and V82 in BON1 and T150, G160, L161 and T188 in BON2.
source: The two BON domains pack against each other via their β-sheets through contacts mediated directly by Y75 and V82 in BON1 and T150, G160, L161 and T188 in BON2 with a total of 38 interdomain NOEs (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR NOE data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and Table 3.

claim: There are a total of 38 interdomain NOEs between the two BON domains.
source: The two BON domains pack against each other via their β-sheets through contacts mediated directly by Y75 and V82 in BON1 and T150, G160, L161 and T188 in BON2 with a total of 38 interdomain NOEs (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Table 3.

claim: The mutation Y75A abolishes DolP function.
source: This interdomain orientation is consistent with SAXS analysis (Figure 2C) and appears to be essential for function as the mutation Y75A abolishes function (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and complementation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Single point mutations G83V and G160V had less effect on function than Y75A, however the double mutant was non-functional.
source: Single point mutations (G83V and G160V) of the highly conserved glycine residues had less effect, however the double mutant was non-functional (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and complementation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The G83V/G160V double mutant protein was not detectable by Western immunoblotting, likely due to structural instability.
source: Since the latter protein was not detectable by Western immunoblotting this is likely due to structural instability (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Simultaneous deletion of dolP and bamB or bamE lead to negative genetic interactions and increased rates of cell lysis.
source: We observed that simultaneous deletion of dolP and bamB or bamE lead to negative genetic interactions and increased rates of cell lysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting a potential interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: No significant interaction could be detected between DolP and the BAM complex through immunoprecipitations.
source: However, despite these genetic interactions, in our hands no significant interaction could be detected between DolP and the BAM complex through immunoprecipitations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and no significant change in overall OMP levels was observed (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No significant change in overall OMP levels was observed in the dolP mutant.
source: However, despite these genetic interactions, in our hands no significant interaction could be detected between DolP and the BAM complex through immunoprecipitations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and no significant change in overall OMP levels was observed (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No apparent differences in LPS profiles were observed between the parent and the dolP mutant.
source: Analyses of purified OM fractions revealed no apparent differences in LPS profiles (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), or phospholipid content (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) between the parent and the dolP mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No apparent differences in phospholipid content were observed between the parent and the dolP mutant.
source: Analyses of purified OM fractions revealed no apparent differences in LPS profiles (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), or phospholipid content (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) between the parent and the dolP mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No significant increase in hepta-acylated Lipid A was observed in the absence of DolP.
source: No significant increase in hepta-acylated Lipid A was observed in the absence of DolP, indicating that the permeability defect is also not due to loss of OM lipid asymmetry (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The permeability defect in dolP mutants is not due to loss of OM lipid asymmetry.
source: No significant increase in hepta-acylated Lipid A was observed in the absence of DolP, indicating that the permeability defect is also not due to loss of OM lipid asymmetry (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Lipid A palmitoylation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ΔdolP cells have an increase in membrane fluidity.
source: In contrast, ΔdolP cells were found to have an increase in membrane fluidity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) as assessed by staining with the membrane intercalating dye pyrene-decanoic acid (PDA), which undergoes a fluorescence shift upon formation of the excimer, an event which is directly related to membrane fluidity (Storek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and a citation.

claim: bamB mutants are sensitive to increased membrane fluidity.
source: Considering that bamB mutants are sensitive to increased membrane fluidity (Storek et al., 2019), these data suggest that the genetic interaction between dolP and bamE or bamB, observed here, is facilitated indirectly through changes to membrane fluidity on the loss of DolP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Storek et al., 2019.

claim: The genetic interaction between dolP and bamE or bamB is facilitated indirectly through changes to membrane fluidity on the loss of DolP.
source: Considering that bamB mutants are sensitive to increased membrane fluidity (Storek et al., 2019), these data suggest that the genetic interaction between dolP and bamE or bamB, observed here, is facilitated indirectly through changes to membrane fluidity on the loss of DolP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of genetic interaction data and membrane fluidity measurements.

claim: DolP bound specifically to micelles containing the anionic phospholipids phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and cardiolipin (CL).
source: DolP bound specifically to micelles containing the anionic phospholipids phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and cardiolipin (CL) but not to micelles devoid of PG or CL, or those containing the zwitterionic phospholipid phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and Figure 4A.

claim: DolP did not bind to micelles devoid of PG or CL, or those containing the zwitterionic phospholipid phosphatidylethanolamine (PE).
source: DolP bound specifically to micelles containing the anionic phospholipids phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and cardiolipin (CL) but not to micelles devoid of PG or CL, or those containing the zwitterionic phospholipid phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and Figure 4A.

claim: Significant CSPs were noted for residues A74, G120-I128, K131-R133, Q135-L137, V142-S145, I173, and S178-V180 upon PG binding.
source: Significant CSPs were noted for A74, G120-I128, K131-R133, Q135-L137, V142-S145, I173, and S178-V180.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The perturbed residues mapped to a single extensive binding site centred on BON2:α1.
source: The perturbed residues were mapped to the structure, revealing a single extensive binding site centred on BON2:α1 that was sufficiently large to contact several lipid molecules (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mapping CSP data onto the structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A dissociation constant (Kd) of ~100 mM (monomeric DHPG) was measured for DolP-PG binding.
source: A dissociation constant (Kd) of ~100 mM (monomeric DHPG) was measured (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: No lipid interaction was seen for any BON1 domain residue.
source: No lipid interaction was seen for any BON1 domain residue, emphasising the specialised role of BON2, which not only differs from DolP BON1, but also from the BON domains of OsmY and Kbp (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 3A and sequence analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: BON1:α1 has a large negative surface potential which is absent in BON2:α1.
source: Analysis of the electrostatic surface reveals a large negative surface potential on BON1:α1, which is absent in BON2:α1 and may act to repel BON1 from PG, whilst BON2:α1 uniquely harbours an aromatic residue W127 in the observed PG- binding site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: BON2:α1 uniquely harbours an aromatic residue W127 in the observed PG-binding site.
source: Analysis of the electrostatic surface reveals a large negative surface potential on BON1:α1, which is absent in BON2:α1 and may act to repel BON1 from PG, whilst BON2:α1 uniquely harbours an aromatic residue W127 in the observed PG- binding site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and sequence comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The amino acids G120-T130 and V132-S139 insert into the micelle interior based on PRE and CSP data.
source: The amino acids G120-T130 and V132-S139 were observed to insert into the micelle interior based on the PRE and CSP data.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR PRE and CSP data used for HADDOCK modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The BON2:α1 helix spans the entirety of the L119-S139 sequence.
source: This reveals an unprecedented burial of the BON2:α1 helix, which spans the entirety of the L119-S139 sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The protein-micelle interface buries 1358 ± 316 Å2.
source: The protein-micelle interface buries 1358 ± 316 Å2 and to our knowledge represents the most extensive structured surface of a membrane:protein interface resolved to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the HADDOCK model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The DolP-micelle interface represents the most extensive structured surface of a membrane:protein interface resolved to date.
source: The protein-micelle interface buries 1358 ± 316 Å2 and to our knowledge represents the most extensive structured surface of a membrane:protein interface resolved to date.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with known structures in the literature.

claim: The side chains of residues G120, S123, W127, T130, and S134 intercalate between the acyl chains.
source: Whilst the side chains of residues G120, S123, W127, T130, and S134 intercalate between the acyl chains, E121, N124, T126, I128, K131, R133, and Q135 buttress the interface (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the HADDOCK model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Residues E121, N124, T126, I128, K131, R133, and Q135 buttress the membrane interface.
source: Whilst the side chains of residues G120, S123, W127, T130, and S134 intercalate between the acyl chains, E121, N124, T126, I128, K131, R133, and Q135 buttress the interface (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the HADDOCK model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutations W127E and L137E are the most critical for DolP function.
source: Mutations within the PG-binding BON2:α1 disrupt the function of DolP, the most critical of which are W127E and L137E; W127 is located in the centre of the binding site that penetrates deep into the core of the PG micelle, and L137 is located at the periphery of the helix (Figure 3B, Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and complementation data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introduction of the W127E mutation abolished binding of DolP to PG micelles.
source: Not only does mutation of W127 lead to loss of function, but introduction of the W127E mutation was shown to abolish binding of DolP to PG micelles as observed by a loss of CSPs within BON2:α1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The helical extension in BON2:α1 contains the W127 anionic phospholipid-binding determinant of DolP.
source: Notably, the BON2:α1 structure presents an extended α-helix when compared to BON1:α1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3). The helical extension in BON2:α1 contains the W127 anionic phospholipid-binding determinant of DolP.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: W127 is absent in BON1 and OsmY.
source: This further implicates W127, which is absent in BON1 and OsmY, in specialisation of DolP BON2 for phospholipid binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Anionic phospholipids demonstrate sub-cellular localisation to sites of higher membrane curvature including the cell poles and division site.
source: DolP binds anionic phospholipid, which demonstrates sub-cellular localisation to sites of higher membrane curvature including the cell poles and division site (Oliver et al., 2014; Renner and Weibel, 2011; Mileykovskaya and Dowhan, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DolP localised specifically to the cell division site.
source: To determine if DolP also shows a preference for such sites, we constructed a plasmid expressing a DolP-mCherry fusion and utilising fluorescence microscopy we observed DolP localised specifically to the cell division site (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DolP is non-functional when targeted to the IM.
source: Considering that DolP is non-functional when targeted to the IM (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), we investigated if DolP could still localise to the site of cell division when it was mistargeted to the IM; no septal localisation was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: DolP mistargeted to the IM showed no septal localisation.
source: Considering that DolP is non-functional when targeted to the IM (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), we investigated if DolP could still localise to the site of cell division when it was mistargeted to the IM; no septal localisation was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Introduction of the W127E mutation abolished division site localisation of DolP.
source: We found that introduction of the W127E mutation, which prevents interaction of DolP with PG/CL micelles, abolished division site localisation of DolP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Division site localisation of DolP is dependent upon binding of DolP to anionic phospholipids.
source: Considering that W127E not only abolished PG/CL binding, but also division site localisation, we concluded that division site localisation of DolP was dependent upon binding of DolP to anionic phospholipids, which have previously been shown to be enriched at the division site (Renner and Weibel, 2011; Mileykovskaya and Dowhan, 2000).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of binding and localization data, supported by citations.

claim: DolP localisation is perturbed in a strain that lacks all three cardiolipin synthases.
source: To confirm this result we analysed DolP localisation in a strain that lacks all three cardiolipin synthases and is defective for cardiolipin synthesis, which was confirmed by phospholipid extraction and thin layer chromatography (Figure 5B). We observed that DolP localisation is perturbed in the CL- strain, with less dividing cells showing localisation of DolP to the septum (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and phospholipid analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Loss of both phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin synthesis worsened the severity of the DolP localisation defect.
source: These effects are further exacerbated in a strain that does not synthesise the major cell anionic phospholipids phosphatidylglycerol or cardiolipin, as confirmed by phospholipid extraction and thin layer chromatography (Figure 5B). Loss of both phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin synthesis worsened the severity of the localisation defect with less septal localisation and a significant proportion of cells showing mislocalisation of DolP to patches at the cell poles (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and phospholipid analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: DolP localisation to the division site is dependent upon interaction with anionic phospholipid via BON2:α1.
source: Taken together these data demonstrate that DolP localisation to the division site is dependent upon interaction with anionic phospholipid via BON2:α1, and that this interaction and the sub-cellular localisation are required for DolP function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of binding, localization, and functional data.

claim: The interaction with anionic phospholipid and the sub-cellular localisation are required for DolP function.
source: Taken together these data demonstrate that DolP localisation to the division site is dependent upon interaction with anionic phospholipid via BON2:α1, and that this interaction and the sub-cellular localisation are required for DolP function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of mutagenesis, binding, localization, and complementation data.

claim: This is the first structure of a dual-BON-domain protein.
source: We have revealed the first structure of a dual-BON-domain protein, a protein architecture that is widely conserved amongst bacteria and therefore provides insight into a diverse range of proteins acting in different organisms.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with existing structural databases.

claim: This is the first evidence for direct binding of lipids by BON domains.
source: We also report the first evidence for direct binding of lipids by BON domains.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with existing literature on BON domains.

claim: DolP BON1 lacks the key W127 phospholipid interaction residue.
source: Interestingly, we detected no phospholipid binding for DolP BON1, which lacks the key W127 phospholipid interaction residue.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data showing no CSPs in BON1 and sequence analysis.

claim: The key W127 residue is also lacking in the other periplasmic BON-domain-containing protein in E. coli, OsmY.
source: This key residue is also lacking in the other periplasmic BON-domain-containing protein in E. coli, OsmY.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: BON domains are not generalist phospholipid-binding domains.
source: Thus, we have demonstrated a specialised role for DolP in the cell and our data suggests BON domains are not generalist phospholipid-binding domains, as was suggested previously (Yeats and Bateman, 2003).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the specificity of DolP BON2 for anionic phospholipids and the lack of binding by BON1, contrasting with previous speculation.

claim: Localisation of DolP to the cell division site is dependent upon recognition of anionic phospholipids by DolP BON2.
source: Here, we show for the first time that localisation of DolP to the cell division site is dependent upon recognition of anionic phospholipids by DolP BON2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combination of binding and localization data.

claim: This is the only example of phospholipid-dependent localization to the bacterial division site.
source: To our knowledge, this is the only example of this mechanism of localisation to the bacterial division site (Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with known mechanisms of division site localization, supported by a citation.

claim: Inhibition of cell constriction by the addition of cephalexin prevents DolP localisation to future division sites.
source: Previous evidence has shown that inhibition of cell constriction, by the addition of cephalexin, also prevents DolP localisation to future division sites (Tsang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsang et al., 2017.

claim: DolP may require cell constriction for localisation to the division site.
source: This indicates that DolP may require cell constriction for localisation to the division site, therefore lending support to the hypothesis that DolP may recognise membrane curvature.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cephalexin experiment cited from Tsang et al., 2017.

claim: DolP function is dependent on localisation to the division site through phospholipid binding and localisation to the OM through its N-terminal lipid anchor.
source: Nevertheless, these data reveal that DolP function is dependent on localisation to the division site through phospholipid binding and localisation to the OM through its N-terminal lipid anchor.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of localization, binding, and complementation data.

claim: The model of DolP localisation provides evidence that anionic phospholipids localise to sites of high membrane curvature in the OM.
source: The model of DolP localisation to the cell division site proposed here also provides some evidence that anionic phospholipids localise to sites of high membrane curvature in the OM.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the DolP localization data and represents a novel observation for the OM.

claim: The OM is significantly different from the IM and is depleted of PG and CL by comparison.
source: Considering that the OM is significantly different from the IM and is depleted of PG and CL by comparison (Lugtenberg and Peters, 1976; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), the localisation of these lipids to sites of negative curvature could be further enhanced by the relative scarcity of these lipids in the OM and this warrants further study.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and by phospholipid analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No direct mechanism through which DolP maintains OM integrity was found.
source: We have not found a direct mechanism through which DolP maintains OM integrity.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the discussion based on the negative results from various assays.

claim: DolP does not influence the OM phospholipid recycling Mla pathway or LPS biogenesis.
source: No differences in LPS content or OM asymmetry were observed in a dolP mutant suggesting DolP does not influence the OM phospholipid recycling Mla pathway or LPS biogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of changes in LPS and phospholipid asymmetry shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: dolP shows synthetic lethality with the gene encoding the periplasmic chaperone SurA.
source: Previous protein:protein interaction studies captured DolP as a near neighbour of two components of the Bam complex, BamD and BamE (Carlson et al., 2019; Babu et al., 2018). Consistent with this, dolP shows synthetic lethality with the gene encoding the periplasmic chaperone SurA, leading to suggestions of a role for DolP in OMP biogenesis (Onufryk et al., 2005; Yan et al., 2019; Typas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: No direct interaction between DolP and the BAM complex was demonstrated.
source: However, we were unable to demonstrate a direct interaction between DolP and the BAM complex, and no such interaction has been seen in the extensive studies evaluating the subunit composition and multimeric states of the BAM complex (Wu et al., 2005; Hagan et al., 2010; Gunasinghe et al., 2018; Knowles et al., 2009) or in similar studies in N. meningitidis (Bos et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunoprecipitation data and citations to previous structural studies of the BAM complex.

claim: DolP is localised to the division site, whereas the Bam complex is uniformly present across the cell surface.
source: However, while this is in agreement with the fact that DolP is localised to the division site, whereas the Bam complex is uniformly present across the cell surface (Gunasinghe et al., 2018), it does not rule out potential transient interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the localization data for DolP and a citation regarding BAM complex localization.

claim: The OM is a rigid structure.
source: Previous observations revealed that the OM is a rigid structure (Rojas et al., 2018) that this membrane rigidity stabilises assembly precincts (Gunasinghe et al., 2018), and that the activity of the BAM complex is sensitive to increases in membrane fluidity (Storek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Membrane rigidity stabilises assembly precincts.
source: Previous observations revealed that the OM is a rigid structure (Rojas et al., 2018) that this membrane rigidity stabilises assembly precincts (Gunasinghe et al., 2018), and that the activity of the BAM complex is sensitive to increases in membrane fluidity (Storek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gunasinghe et al., 2018.

claim: The activity of the BAM complex is sensitive to increases in membrane fluidity.
source: Previous observations revealed that the OM is a rigid structure (Rojas et al., 2018) that this membrane rigidity stabilises assembly precincts (Gunasinghe et al., 2018), and that the activity of the BAM complex is sensitive to increases in membrane fluidity (Storek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Storek et al., 2019.

claim: The increased membrane fluidity of dolP cells provides a challenging environment for assembly precincts to be maintained.
source: We suggest that the increased membrane fluidity of the dolP cells, demonstrated here, provides a challenging environment for assembly precincts to be maintained.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the membrane fluidity data and cited literature on BAM complex sensitivity.

claim: DolP might modulate peptidoglycan remodeling to minimise the clash between the periplasmic components of the assembly precinct and the cell wall.
source: We hypothesise that DolP, perhaps through interactions with peptidoglycan amidases (Tsang et al., 2017), might also modulate peptidoglycan remodeling in such a way as to minimise the clash between the periplasmic components of the assembly precinct and the cell wall, which might be exacerbated in regions of high membrane curvature.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the genetic connection to amidases and the localization data.

claim: Loss of DolP increases sensitivity to antibiotics and membrane disrupting agents.
source: The demonstration that loss of DolP increases sensitivity to antibiotics and membrane disrupting agents, in addition to the decrease in virulence in vivo, and an increase of the efficacy of the N. meningitidis vaccine, suggests DolP will provide a useful starting platform for antimicrobial design based on the disruption to regulation of multiple envelope biogenesis mechanisms (Morris et al., 2018; Giuliani et al., 2006; Pizza et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Loss of DolP leads to a decrease in virulence in vivo.
source: The demonstration that loss of DolP increases sensitivity to antibiotics and membrane disrupting agents, in addition to the decrease in virulence in vivo, and an increase of the efficacy of the N. meningitidis vaccine, suggests DolP will provide a useful starting platform for antimicrobial design based on the disruption to regulation of multiple envelope biogenesis mechanisms (Morris et al., 2018; Giuliani et al., 2006; Pizza et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DolP increases the efficacy of the N. meningitidis vaccine.
source: The demonstration that loss of DolP increases sensitivity to antibiotics and membrane disrupting agents, in addition to the decrease in virulence in vivo, and an increase of the efficacy of the N. meningitidis vaccine, suggests DolP will provide a useful starting platform for antimicrobial design based on the disruption to regulation of multiple envelope biogenesis mechanisms (Morris et al., 2018; Giuliani et al., 2006; Pizza et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DolP will provide a useful starting platform for antimicrobial design.
source: The demonstration that loss of DolP increases sensitivity to antibiotics and membrane disrupting agents, in addition to the decrease in virulence in vivo, and an increase of the efficacy of the N. meningitidis vaccine, suggests DolP will provide a useful starting platform for antimicrobial design based on the disruption to regulation of multiple envelope biogenesis mechanisms (Morris et al., 2018; Giuliani et al., 2006; Pizza et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications based on the findings.
